one_line: Midam Kim (ServiceNow) uses a linguistics framework to explain why voice agents fail and proposes diagnosing them by listen/speak channels, timing, and the user's mental model.
summary: Midam Kim, an ML engineer at ServiceNow, opens with a voice-bot call where spelling, account-number capture and turn-taking all broke, and the bot never tried interactive clarification. He frames voice AI as a joint activity between two parties, the way human conversation is, rather than a one-way pipeline. His framework has two channels (listening and speaking) crossed with four layers: sounds, words, interaction (turn timing) and mental model (task intent). He argues these layers are interdependent and must be aligned, and that the conversation runs on a timeline where only the user's evolving mental model persists after the audio is gone. He lists engineering levers (ASR/TTS choice and pre/post-processing, vocabulary, turn detection, emotion handling, dynamic context retention) and says business metrics such as escalations and abandoned calls follow from linguistic failures. He points to ServiceNow's EvaBench as a way to diagnose a voice agent, and closes by saying speakers adapt and languages change, so systems must keep up. The talk gives a diagnostic lens but no fixes or measured results.

key_ideas.idea: Voice agent failures are linguistic failures, shown through a real call.
key_ideas.detail: A bot misheard M vs N in a spelled name, applied English-centric TTS reading rules to the spelling, cut the user off during an account number, and then asked for a repeat without trying clarification. The user asked for a human.

key_ideas.idea: Treat voice AI as a joint activity, not a pipeline.
key_ideas.detail: Human conversation is two parties taking turns and updating shared mental models. The speaker says users expect this same mutual process from bots.

key_ideas.idea: Use a two-channel by four-layer grid to locate failures.
key_ideas.detail: Listening and speaking channels each have sounds (recognition or pronunciation), words (understanding or word choice), interaction (turn timing), and mental model (intent or the information the user needs).

key_ideas.idea: The layers are interdependent and must be aligned.
key_ideas.detail: Good sounds depend on word-level handling, which depends on turn-taking, which is needed for task completion. Missing any one layer makes the agent fail.

key_ideas.idea: Voice is silently tracked on a timeline, so only the mental model persists.
key_ideas.detail: Unlike chat, spoken words leave no visible history. The user's evolving mental model is the only thing that remembers the call, so it is the thing to manage.

key_ideas.idea: Satisfaction levers are dynamic, not one-off settings.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker lists ASR and TTS choice with pre- and post-processing, shared vocabulary, turn detection and latency, emotion handling, and context retention. All of these need to adjust during the call and fit different users, including unhappy ones.

key_ideas.idea: Linguistic quality links directly to business metrics.
key_ideas.detail: Better handling should lower user frustration, task failures, live-agent escalations, abandoned calls, and silent failures. The speaker says business implications are linguistic implications.

key_ideas.idea: Speakers adapt and languages drift, so systems need to keep up.
key_ideas.detail: Users adapt to the agent during a call and across calls. The speaker asks whether a system will still fit language change within months.

techniques.name: Linguistic diagnostic grid for voice agents
techniques.how: Score each failure on channel (listen or speak) times layer (sounds, words, interaction, mental model) to find which layer broke, rather than blaming the whole pipeline.
techniques.when: When debugging a voice agent or auditing a call transcript to decide whether the ASR, TTS, turn-taking or task logic is at fault.

techniques.name: Interactive clarification on recognition errors
techniques.how: When the bot is unsure of a spelled name or an identifier, it confirms the specific uncertain item (for example, asking about M vs N) instead of repeating the whole request or silently proceeding.
techniques.when: For spelled names, account numbers and other identifiers where ASR errors are common.

techniques.name: Locale-aware pre-processing for TTS and vocabulary
techniques.how: Curate a shared vocabulary and pre-process text so that spelled letters, codes and names are not read with default English rules.
techniques.when: When the agent reads back names, spelled strings or codes that the default TTS pronounces wrongly.

techniques.name: Turn-taking and barge-in control
techniques.how: Tune turn detection and latency so the bot does not cut the user off mid-number and only speaks when it is its turn.
techniques.when: When users read long strings such as account numbers, or pause while thinking.

techniques.name: Dynamic per-call context retention
techniques.how: Keep track of the user's current intent and known facts across the timeline, and adapt the style for different users and emotional states during the call.
techniques.when: For long multi-turn voice calls where users get frustrated or change plans mid-call.

techniques.name: EvaBench for diagnosing voice agents
techniques.how: Run ServiceNow's EvaBench, a speech-to-speech benchmark, to diagnose a voice agent's status across the framework layers.
techniques.when: When you need a structured voice-agent eval before tuning ASR, TTS or turn-taking.

hot_takes: Voice is called the most natural interface, but it is actually hard, and a bad voice bot fails catastrophically.
Business implications of voice AI are linguistic implications, so hire linguists as well as engineers.
Only the user's mental model persists in a voice call, so context management matters more than the audio pipeline.

relevance.why: No voice or speech component in the AgentOS layers listed in the profile.
No checkpoint, planning, loop or approval content relevant to the Claude Code harness.
The layer-by-channel grid could serve as a rubric for failure analysis in any conversational agent eval, including chat.
relevance.action: Try a listen/speak x sounds/words/interaction/mental-model tagging pass on a sample of failed transcripts from an existing agent eval to see whether the grid surfaces failure modes that a flat error label misses.
